subject: English
topic: Direct and Indirect Speech — Tense Backshift and Special Forms (W10 B2)

questions.stem:
Change to Indirect Speech:
'I live in Delhi,' he said.

options.option_text: He said that he lives in Delhi.
He said that he lived in Delhi.
He told that he lived in Delhi.
He said that he is living in Delhi.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Simple present 'live' → simple past 'lived' (tense backshift in indirect speech when reporting verb is past). Trap: option A keeps present tense (no backshift); option C wrongly uses 'told' without an indirect object ('told him that' would be correct, but 'told that' alone is not standard); option D shifts to past continuous unnecessarily.

questions.stem:
Change to Indirect Speech:
'I will help you,' she promised.

options.option_text: She promised that she will help me.
She promised that she would help me.
She promised that she has helped me.
She promised to help me.

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Will' → 'would' (modal backshift). The pronoun 'you' changes to 'me' (shift from 2nd to 1st person perspective). Option D ('promised to help me') is also structurally acceptable in standard English for a promise, but option B preserves the original sentence structure with the 'that' clause, which is what is tested in SSC. Trap: option A keeps 'will' (no modal backshift).

questions.stem:
Change to Indirect Speech:
'Are you coming to the party?' Ravi asked Priya.

options.option_text: Ravi asked Priya if she was coming to the party.
Ravi asked Priya if she is coming to the party.
Ravi asked Priya that she was coming to the party.
Ravi asked Priya whether she came to the party.

questions.explanation: A is correct. For yes/no questions in indirect speech: use 'if' or 'whether' (not 'that'); invert the question to statement order; apply tense backshift. 'Are you coming' → 'if she was coming' (present continuous → past continuous; 'you' → 'she'). Trap: option C uses 'that' (only used for statements); option D backshifts too far ('came' is simple past, not the continuous needed).

questions.stem:
Change to Indirect Speech:
The teacher said, 'Honesty is the best policy.'

options.option_text: The teacher said that honesty was the best policy.
The teacher said honesty was the best policy.
The teacher said that honesty is the best policy.
The teacher told that honesty is the best policy.

questions.explanation: C is correct. When a direct speech contains a UNIVERSAL TRUTH or proverb, the tense does NOT change in indirect speech — it remains present tense. 'Honesty is the best policy' is a universal truth; therefore 'is' stays as 'is'. Trap: options A and B wrongly backshift to 'was'; option D uses 'told' incorrectly (needs an object: 'told them').

questions.stem:
Change to Indirect Speech:
'Please open the window,' she requested.

options.option_text: She requested to open the window.
She requested that the window is opened.
She requested him to open the window.
She requested him that he should open the window.

questions.explanation: C is correct. Imperatives in indirect speech: 'say/request' + object + 'to + infinitive'. 'Please open' becomes 'requested him to open'. 'Please' is dropped (it is a politeness marker, not content). Trap: option A omits the indirect object (who is being requested); option D adds 'that he should' which is acceptable in some styles but 'to + infinitive' is the standard concise SSC form.

questions.stem:
Convert to Direct Speech:
He asked me where I had been the previous night.

options.option_text: He asked, 'Where have you been yesterday night?'
He asked, 'Where were you the previous night?'
He asked, 'Where had you been last night?'
He asked, 'Where were you last night?'

questions.explanation: C is correct. Converting from indirect to direct: past perfect 'had been' → what is the original? 'had been' (past perfect in indirect) corresponds to past perfect in the original question too (or simple past). 'Previous night' → 'last night'. The original question: 'Where had you been last night?' (he is asking about an event that happened before another past reference). 'You' (he asked me = 2nd person in direct). Trap: 'yesterday night' is non-standard (should be 'last night'); option D shifts to simple past ('were') losing the perfect aspect.

questions.stem:
Change to Indirect Speech:
'What a beautiful garden!' she exclaimed.

options.option_text: She exclaimed that what a beautiful garden it was.
She exclaimed that the garden was very beautiful.
She exclaimed the garden was a beautiful one.
She exclaimed saying what a beautiful garden.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Exclamatory sentences in indirect speech: drop the exclamation, use a reporting verb like 'exclaimed that', and convert 'What a + adj + noun!' to 'the noun was very adjective.' Rule: What a beautiful garden → the garden was very beautiful. Tense backshift: is (implied) → was. Trap: option A retains the exclamatory 'What' structure which is incorrect in indirect speech; option C loses the 'very' intensifier.

questions.stem:
Change to Indirect Speech:
'May you live long!' the elder blessed the child.

options.option_text: The elder blessed the child that he may live long.
The elder blessed the child saying that he might live long.
The elder blessed the child to live long.
The elder said the child might live long.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Optative sentences (blessings, wishes) in indirect speech: use 'wished/prayed/blessed' + 'that' + 'might'. 'May' → 'might' (backshift of modal). 'You' → 'he' (third person). Option D loses the blessing verb and sounds like a prediction rather than a blessing. Trap: option A keeps 'may' (no backshift); option C converts to infinitive (loses the blessing nuance).

questions.stem:
Change to Indirect Speech:
He said, 'I have been working since morning and I am very tired.'

options.option_text: He said that he had been working since morning and he is very tired.
He said that he was working since morning and he was very tired.
He said that he had been working since morning and he was very tired.
He said that he has been working since morning and he was very tired.

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'I have been working' (present perfect continuous) → 'he had been working' (past perfect continuous). 'I am tired' (simple present) → 'he was tired' (simple past). Both clauses undergo backshift consistently. 'Since morning' stays unchanged (it is a time expression, not a reference pronoun). Trap: option B changes 'had been working' to 'was working' (drops perfect aspect); option D uses 'has been' (no backshift).

questions.stem:
Change to Indirect Speech:
'Don't make noise,' the librarian warned the students.

options.option_text: The librarian warned the students don't make noise.
The librarian warned the students not to make noise.
The librarian warned the students that they not make noise.
The librarian told the students to not make noise.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Negative imperatives in indirect speech: 'Don't + verb' → 'not to + verb'. Full form: warned/told/ordered + object + 'not to + infinitive'. Trap: option D splits 'to not make' (split infinitive, acceptable in modern use but not preferred in SSC). Option C uses 'that they not' (subjunctive — rare and not the standard SSC conversion form). Always use 'not to + base verb' for negative imperatives.
